content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to train representations equivariant to data augmentations by optimizing two additional regularizers together with the standard cross-entropy loss. Specifically, equivariance is promoted by minimizing the L2 loss between the embedding transformed by $M_a$ and embedding obtained by feeding augmented data, and uniformity is forced to reduce invariance. Experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

+ The idea of promoting equivariance to data augmentations seems interesting and useful.

Weaknesses

- Steerability is not inspired/explained well. Throughout the description on the method in Section 3, "steer" is never used, except when combining loss to argue that the final loss is to train a steerable model. What is steerability in deep representations, how does the proposed loss promote steerability, and how are steerability and equivariance related? It seems the authors do not distinguish steerability and equivariance well.

- There are prior works about training equivariant networks. How do the authors compare them with this work? There are many properties that models can be equivariant, and it seems this work is limited to learning to be equivariant to data augmentations only.

- How does the embedding map M look like? I couldn't find the actually experimented version throughout the paper.

- Experimental comparisons are limited to vanilla ResNet-50 training vs. proposed method. For example, I wonder how the proposed method is compared to existing methods for enhancing robustness/detecting out-of-distribution detection in Table 3. Given that the proposed method is orthogonal to them, it would be interesting to see if the combined method can improve the performance further.

- Experimental setting is limited to ImageNet-C. Experiments on standard OOD detection benchmarks might also be interesting.

- I couldn't find ablation studies on the choice/combination of hyperparameters/losses.

- Typo: 2nd and 3rd rows of Figure 1 have the same metric.

- Typo: $e(g_a(x)$ at the end of Section 3.3.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Writing is clear and well-written in general, except for confusion between steerability and equivariance. Equivariant and/or steerable deep learning is not novel. The code is not shared but they claimed that the code will be released.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The idea is interesting, but the experimental setting is quite limited to show the effectiveness of the proposed method. Also, I recommend authors distinguish steerability and equivariance in a better way. Please answer my concerns above.

**post-rebuttal**

The authors partially addressed my concerns, so my initial rating is unchanged. Below are additional comments:

- It is not clear if the mapping on the embedding space $M$ behaves as expected. How do you guarantee that nonlinear and complex data augmentations on the data space can always be simplified to be linear transformations on the embedding space (given that the actual implementation of $M$ is essentially the summation of the linearly transformed embedding vector and augmentation parameter vector)? I think more experimental analyses other than a few number of image retrieval results are required to make the results more convincing.

- Scalability on the size of model and dataset is still questionable; author response did not address this.

- Together with scalability, it would be interesting to see if hyperparameters ($\alpha$ and $\beta$) are sensitive to the choice on the model and dataset.

content.title: Author response to Reviewer EeNj
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their careful review and questions. We address comments below:

- “Steerability is not inspired/explained well”:  
We apologize for the lack of clarity in definition and distinction between steerability and equivariance. We have added more explanation for steerability in section 3.2. We also refer the reviewer to section A.1 for a visual depiction of these concepts. 
- “Prior Works”:  
Our work is complementary to prior work that encourages equivariance via architectural modifications, which are usually restricted to particular transformations (e.g. rotation); we highlight them in our related work. We do indeed restrict ourselves to increasing equivariance through augmentations, but augmentations are a fundamental part of deep learning (both supervised and self-supervised) and thus we believe that this approach has a lot of practical benefits.
- “How does the embedding map M look like?”:  The structure of $M$ is detailed in Section 3.2.
- “Experimental comparisons are limited”:  
We thank the reviewer for recognizing that our method can fuel further improvements in robustness and OOD settings. We do agree that our method is orthogonal to existing approaches and can be combined with them for even better results. However, our paper focuses on studying equivariance and its benefits as opposed to current invariance-based techniques. Combining it with prior work is outside the scope of this current submission.
- “Ablations”:   
We have conducted ablations for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ parameters and added a section the Appendix (section A.3, page 15).
- “Typo: 2nd and 3rd rows of Figure 1 have the same metric”:  
The rows do indeed both use the same representation, $\Delta M(e(x))$, but for different values of $\theta$ for the transformations (pink vs orange, or dark vs light).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes steerable equivariant embedding for representation learning. Unlike invariant embedding typically achieved through learning with data augmentation, the model jointly learns a feature embedding and a (NN-parametrized) latent space transformation. Equivariant embedding is achieved by minimizing the cross-entropy loss regularized by the equivariance-promoting regularizer and the uniformity regularizer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
1. The paper is generally well-written.
2. Extensive experiments have been conducted.

**Weakness**
1. Equation (2) is misleading. Instead of $g_a(x, \theta_a)$ and $M_a(e(x), \theta_a)$, the notations $g(x, \theta_a)$ and $M(e(x), \theta_a)$ should be used, since, if I understand correctly, the mapping $M$ and $g$ depends on $a$ only through $\theta_a$.
2. Instead of using $L_U$ and $L_E$ as two regularization terms, why not use $\rho_a$ directly? The authors mentioned that pushing $e(x)$ and $e(g_a(x))$ apart destabilizes training. However, isn't pushing them apart what the authors aim to achieve?
3. Equation (4) and Equation (5) are a bit confusing. What are $x_i$ and $x_j$ in the definition of $L_U(x)$? Is $x$ a batch of data containing $x_i$ and $x_j$?
4. What happens if the number of transformations $a$ is large in equation (5)? For example, consider the cyclical group $C_8$; does that mean the loss $L_E$ will be the sum of eight terms?
5. What is SimCLR at the bottom of page 5?
6. The comparison between the invariant and the proposed equivariant embedding (especially in Section 4.1, table 1) seems unfair and somewhat pointless. After all, the invariant embedding is trained (through augmentation) to be invariant, and thus freezing the encoder while training $M$ with equation (3) will essentially learn an identity map. This surely leads to a large $\rho_a$ defined in equation (2). What I am trying to say is that invariant embedding is indeed doing its job correctly, and it is pointless to compare it to the proposed model by forcing it to learn an $M$.
7. In section 4.2, how is $w_n$ decided? Again, the invariant model is doing its job correctly. From a different point of view, one might say that the invariant model in Figure 2 is robustly retrieving the same figure after input transformation, whereas the figures retrieved by the proposed embedding actually seem arbitrary.
8 What is $r_i$ in MRR? How is it calculated?
9. More explanation is needed for Figure 2, 3, 4, 5. For the first row $e(x)$, are they the retrieved image from the same query? Does it mean the authors have trained multiple embedding models?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally well-written. Learning an equivariant embedding is interesting, and jointly learning $M$ and $e$ is original.
content.summary_of_the_review: Even though the paper tries to address an interesting question, there are many issued identified in the *weakness* part of this review. There is also no theoretical contribution in the paper.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5674 by Reviewer nTJZ

content.title: Author response to Reviewer nTJZ
content.comment:
We thank you for your time and review. We believe that there has been a significant misunderstanding of our work. We respond to your concerns below:

- “Equation (2) is misleading”:  
To clarify, for each augmentation we have a separate $M_a$, which is parametrized by $\theta_a$. Furthermore, each augmentation at input is denoted by $g_a$, which is parametrized by $\theta_a$. So removing the $a$ for $M$ and $g$ would be inaccurate.
- “Use equivariance measure as loss”:  
What we meant by “destabilize training” is that the cross-entropy loss would drop when using $\rho_a$ directly; thus the quality of the embedding would drop, which is not desirable. We found $L_U$ and $L_E$ much easier to control. We think this is because $\rho_a$ is set up as a ratio of terms which we have found to be unstable in our experience.
- “Equation (4) and Equation (5) are a bit confusing”:  
Yes, $x_i$ and $x_j$ are different elements of a batch of data (as stated below Equation (4)). Note that the batch also contains the augmentation for each sample $x_i$, which is shown as $g_a(x_i)$. We have a uniformity loss over unaugmented and augmented samples which is what is shown in Equation (5).
- “What happens if the number of transformations a is large in equation (5)”:   
The term $L_E$ is dependent on the number of different augmentations; not the number of potential member transformations within an augmentation. Thus for crop and color, we have that $L_E$ consists of only two terms.
- “What is SimCLR at the bottom of page 5?”:  We have added a citation.
- “Comparison between invariant and the proposed equivariant embedding...seems unfair and somewhat pointless”:   
The purpose of our paper is to propose a regularizer to encourage equivariance and steerability and demonstrate the benefits. If certain properties such as steered retrieval are of interest (e.g. Figures 1-3), then it is not possible to do that with an invariance-promoting loss. The purpose of the experiments are to empirically demonstrate this benefit. This is not to say that an invariant embedding is doing its job incorrectly, indeed we demonstrate that an invariant embedding doing its job correctly is not beneficial for the applications we note. Hence, we believe that such comparisons are not pointless.
- “In section 4.2, how is $w_n$ decided”:  
As we mention, we chosen $w_n$ empirically based on a balance between semantic retrieval and visual retrieval. Pushing too far in one direction (making $w_n$ too large) would override all semantic information.  
In Figure 1-3, all retrieved results for the equivariant model come from the same ImageNet class, thus they are not arbitrary. However, the equivariant model is able to prioritize color over shape, which may be desirable in this context (e.g. if you are interested in retrieving flowers or dresses of a certain color). There is no ability to perform such a retrieval with an invariant model since it is insensitive to color.
- “What is $r_i$ in MRR?” :  
As mentioned in the paper, $r_i$ is the rank of the desired result within a list of responses. We always have the correct desired result in our queried database, and $r_i$ is simply calculated by measuring its rank in the list of retrieved nearest neighbors (for e.g. it is 1 if it is the nearest neighbor, 2 for the second nearest, and so on).
- “More explanation is needed for Figure 2, 3, 4, 5.”:  
For all these figures we have only two models: an invariant one and an equivariant one. The row marked e(x) consists of retrievals using the embedding of the original query image x. The other rows use the embedding of the transformed image e(g(x)) (g is the transformation) or a transformation in embedding space M(e(x)). We refer the reviewer to section 4.2 for an explanation of the queries.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for learning equivariant representations with respect to photometric/geometric transformations, which has received little attention in the equivariant learning literature. The representations are also designed to be steerable so that the transformations can be directly applied in the latent space. The implementation of the method is simple and intuitive in that a mapping between two embeddings is introduced given an augmentation and regularized to be equivariant by a loss function. Since the augmentations are performed in the latent space through the mapping function, it brings significant speedup (nearly 50x) for test-time augmentations, and the equivariance of the mapping facilitates an interesting application for image retrieval, which works with image augmentations. At last, the paper demonstrates the method is beneficial to transfer learning and out-of-detection tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper has strength in novelty since it might be the first work incorporating transformations other than matrix groups for equivariant learning. In addition, it has shown the steerability and equivariance of the representations are highly practical and effective in several tasks and applications. However, the exposition of the proposed method still lacks in the following aspects:

1) The statement “Our method is generalizable across architectures and pre-training losses.” on page 2 has not been proven empirically, as the authors only employ ResNet and cross-entropy loss for experiments.

2) The authors, on page 3, claim the proposed method is widely applicable as long as a transformation is parameterized in input space and this covers the specific transformations, i.e., rotation, that the prior work mainly concentrates on. But I am not convinced about the generalizability of the method to those specific transformations and ask for evidence.

3) The proposed method applies the same augmentation for invariant and equivariant learning, and the uniformity regularizer is proposed to resolve this conflict. But I could not find any ablation studies for this regularizer and sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters \alpha and \beta. In addition, I want to ask why the independent views for equivariance and uniformity losses are used, making them inconsistent with Eq. (5). Please answer these points with experimental results.

4) The ρ value for the equivariant model in Table 1 seems to be still large as the model is trained with exactly the same loss function as the measurement. Can you provide the curve for the numerator (equivariance metric), the denominator (invariance metric), and the value itself separately over the course of training?

5) In Figure 5, the order of retrieved images for e(g(x)) and M(e(x)) are opposite to each other, which is supposed to be the same in general as in Figure 14. What is the reason for this one? In some figures, the right parenthesis is missing.

6) Table 3 is not referred to in any part of the paper, and the values are not the same as that of Table 4. Please explain the difference between them. 

7) For OOD in Figure 6, I want to see the results further when input data is explicitly forwarded with 60 augmentations for both invariant and equivariant models to identify the upper bound though the time is consumed significantly.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is clear, but I would recommend making a compact description for notations (explanation for Eq. (1)) and equations (does not seem to need two separate equations in Eq. (5)). Both the novelty and reproducibility are good as the proposed method provides a new direction for equivariant learning and is also simple to implement.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This work is novel in its idea and direction, but it significantly lacks investigations on the method itself, as I commented on the weaknesses. 
Since the authors' response addresses some of my concerns, I raise my rating, leaning toward weak accept.

content.title: Author response to Reviewer k3c6
content.comment:
We thank you for your time and constructive feedback. We are also happy to note that you find our work novel. As far as we are aware, ours is the first work to show the benefits of steerability in the setting of standard architecture and training losses. New changes to the paper are marked in a different color. We respond to the reviewer's comments below:

- “The statement on page 2 has not been proven empirically”:  
We agree with the reviewer that the statement “Our method is generalizable across architectures" and have removed it from the paper until we have new results on other architectures and pre-training losses. With limited time and compute during the rebuttal period, we hope to do so for the final version of the paper.
- Evidence for rotation augmentation:  
As requested, we have added rotation to the current list of augmentations and provide the results in Appendix A.4, and table 5. We see that the $\rho$ value of rotation (equivariance measure) is lower for our model than a standard (invariant) ResNet-50 in this case as well, and that the existing model accuracy and $\rho$ values for other augmentations are minimally affected. This confirms that our proposed method generalizes to rotations as well.
- Ablations for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ parameters:  
We have conducted ablations for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ parameters and added a section the Appendix (section A.3, page 15).   
We apologize for the confusion about the views: we do indeed use the same views for both losses and not independent ones. 
- “The $\rho$ value for the equivariant model in Table 1 seems to be still large”:  
To clarify: the model is not trained with the same loss as our equivariant measurement: it is in fact only trained with the numerator. We have added the requested curves to the Appendix section A.2, Figure 8.
- “In Figure 5, the order of retrieved images”:   
Our model and maps are imperfect (as evidenced by non-zero $\rho$), so the ordering w.r.t to an $M(e(x))$ query is not exactly equal to the ordering for $e(g(x))$ in all cases. We did not cherry pick perfect results, and so Figure 5 indeed references an imperfect example in which the ordering is flipped w.r.t crop/zoom. Nevertheless, in figure 14 in the appendix $M(e(x))$  attains the same order as $e(g(x))$, which depicts the correct results for this query. We apologize for the confusion, and to minimize it for future readers we swap figure 5 and 14, and move the erroneous example to the appendix. 
- “Table 3 is not referred to in any part of the paper”: 
We apologize for this oversight, we have added a reference to table 3 in the Section 4.4. We also erroneously failed to indicate that the values in Table 3 are averaged across different severities, and not only for severity 3. We have fixed this. Additionally, we have updated the values in table 3 to be aggregated over all 5 severities, instead of only 1,3, and 5.
- Experiments with input augmentation:  
 We have added the requested experiment to the Appendix (section A.5). We applied up to 8 input augmentations (we were unable to fit more into memory without significantly reducing batch size). It is seen that (1) in general input augmentations do better than embedding space augmentations, however at a significantly higher compute (50x slower) and memory cost; and (2) equivariant input augmentations always do better than invariant input. This shows the benefit of our equivariance promoting regularizer.
- "compact description for notations":   
We have merged the two equations in Eq. 5 for better readability. We have also made the explanation for Eq. 1 more concise.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method to learn equivariant representations that are steerable by a learned function in representation space. They empirically demonstrate the method as an improvement to ImageNet classification, where the pre-trained model performs better in transfer, retrieval, corruption, OOD detection settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

1. The idea is interesting and intuitive. Experiments are convincing.
2. The retrieval visualization is compelling. It clearly shows the property of the feature space learned by the proposed method compared with invariant learning.
3. The test-time augmentation is a useful application.

Weakness
1. The scope is limited to supervised ImageNet classification, while the self-supervised setting can be more appealing. As the paper claims, the approach “is general and easily extends to self-supervised settings”, it is relatively straightforward to try this in a contrastive learning setting (e.g., just remove the supervised loss)? If there was an issue with the contrastive learning setting, could the authors discuss it?
2. How does this method compare with the inverse-prediction style method as in Xiao et al., 2021, Dangovski et al., 2022? Which is more effective? I feel their methods can also be easily extended to the supervised setting -- just attach a loss with an inverse predictor.
3. How to determine alpha and beta in the loss? I have earlier noticed that increasing uniformity alone (alpha=0, beta>0) can sometimes improve transfer and robustness.

Minor: The citation should use \citet instead of \citep in some places.

content.title: Author response to reviewer D95j
content.comment:
We thank you for taking the time to review our paper carefully and the constructive suggestions. We note that our paper is the first (as far as we are aware) to show the benefits of encouraging and applying steerability in embedding space (as noted by reviewer k3c6). We respond to the reviewer's concerns below:

- “Try with contrastive learning self-supervised loss”:  
It should indeed be relatively straightforward to try our method in a contrastive learning setting by adding our equivariance-promoting regularizers to a contrastive loss. Compute constraints in the rebuttal period (contrastive learning takes significantly more training epochs) means that we will update these results as compute becomes available. We note, however, that supervised pre-training is still very widely used for transfer learning and other tasks and therefore our results would already be of interest to the community. 

- “Compare with the inverse-prediction style method as in Xiao et al., 2021, Dangovski et al., 2022?”:   
The method of Xiao et. al. heavily relies on creating positive and negative samples for augmentations and manipulating their ‘distances’ with the contrastive loss. A-priori, it is unclear how this can be extended to the supervised setting. We agree that the predictor from Dangovski et al. can probably be used in the supervised setting. But, as noted in our paper, it does so without the creation of any equivalent steerable maps and thus cannot be used for the many applications of steerability that we demonstrate in the paper. 

- “How to determine $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in the loss?”: We have empirically selected alpha and beta values such that (1) the cross-entropy accuracy is not reduced; and (2) the equivariance values are reduced below 1 for all augmentations. We add an ablation study for these in the appendix (section A.3, page 15). We are not aware of any work studying transfer and robustness improvements by simply adding a uniformity regularizer. We would be thankful to the reviewer if they could draw our attention to such a study. Nevertheless, we try these hyperparameter choices and record transfer performance in Table 7 in the Appendix (page 17). We see that out of the 3 choices tried, one does give higher transfer performance than both the invariant and equivariant baselines. However, they all have $\rho$ values pointing to invariance, and thus adding uniformity alone does not impart equivariance to the representations.

content.title: Author response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for the time taken to provide thorough reviews of the paper. We wish to highlight the fact that we demonstrate a novel method for increasing equivariance to augmentations in representations, and as noted by reviewer k3c6 are the first work to incorporate transformations other than matrix groups. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to also introduce the idea of doing so directly by learning equivariant maps and not indirect methods such as inverse transformation-prediction. This imparts us the novel advantage of employing steerability to further increase the applications of equivariant representations, such as for retrieval, robustness and transfer learning.

We have incorporated reviewer comments into our paper, and highlighted all new additions in the colour violet for easy perusal. We add hyperparameter ablations, extend on the OOD experiments with input augmentations, add mCE calculations for robustness comparisons, and test the generalization of our method to rotation transformations among other changes.  We hope that these further experiments will convince the reviewers of the quality and importance of our contribution.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
Paper Summary - The paper extends widely-used invariant representation learning to more general equivariant learning that is also steerable or controllable by a learned function in the representation space. This is achieved by optimizing additional loss functions (the equivariance-promoting regularizer and the uniformity regularizer) together with the standard cross-entropy loss, without the need of changing the model architecture. Equivariance is promoted by minimizing the L2 loss between the transformed embedding and the embedding obtained by feeding augmented data. The equivariance-promoting regularizer is claimed to be general, and mainly integrated into supervised pre-training. Photometric and geometric transformations are the main focus of the paper. Experimental results demonstrate improved representations for tasks such as image retrieval, robustness, transfer learning, and out-of-distribution detection.


Strengths and Weaknesses - While the reviewers recognize that the paper presents an interesting idea for equivariant representation learning with a simple, intuitive implementation, they also have various concerns regarding the original submission and the revised paper. First, a major issue is that the paper is claimed to be very general across architectures and pre-training losses in the original submission, but the actual empirical evaluation is of limited scope. The revision changes the tone a little bit. But the reviewers feel that the experiments are still unconvincing. Importantly, as the reviewers point out, while invariant representation learning is a central concept in self-supervised learning, this paper focuses on integrating the proposed equivariance-promoting loss in the supervised setting. It would be of broader impact if such a loss had been investigated in the self-supervised setting as well. Also, only the ResNet-50 architecture, cross-entropy loss, and specific transformations have been studied. Second, some important baselines are missing, such as the inverse-prediction style method (Xiao et al., 2021, Dangovski et al., 2022) as pointed out by the reviewers, making the comparisons unfair. Third, more in-depth analysis about the model behavior and scalability is missing.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The authors’ rebuttal clarified some confusion like the imprecise definition of steerability and hyper-parameter sensitivity, but failed to address the major concerns as mentioned above. So I cannot recommend acceptance based on the current version.
